content: Oral analgesics are a commonly used and convenient method for managing pain after a caesarean section. These medications can be administered alone or in combination with other forms of pain relief. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness of oral analgesics for post-caesarean pain management. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared oral analgesics to placebo, no treatment, or other oral medications. A total of eight small trials involving 962 women contributed data to the analysis, although only four of these trials were considered to have a low risk of bias. None of the included studies reported on the primary outcome of adequate pain relief. 1. Opioid Analgesics vs. Placebo One trial with 120 women found no significant difference between opioids and placebo in terms of the need for additional pain relief (risk ratio [RR] 0.33, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.06 to 1.92). The effect of opioids on adverse drug effects was uncertain (RR 6.58, 95% CI 0.38 to 113.96). Low-dose (75 mg) and high-dose (150 mg) tramadol showed no significant difference in the need for additional pain relief (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.12 to 3.78 and RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.68, respectively, one study, 80 women). 2. Non-Opioid Analgesics vs. Placebo The need for additional pain relief was lower in the non-opioid group, but the confidence interval was wide, indicating uncertainty (average RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.01, six studies, 584 women). Substantial heterogeneity was observed due to the variety of non-opioid drugs used (I² = 85%). Gabapentin was the only non-opioid drug that significantly reduced the need for additional pain relief (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.51, one trial, 126 women). Other non-opioid drugs, such as celecoxib, ibuprofen, ketoprofen, naproxen, and paracetamol, showed no significant difference compared to placebo. Maternal side effects were more common with non-opioid analgesics (RR 11.12, 95% CI 2.13 to 58.22, two trials, 267 women). Gabapentin at doses of 300 mg (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.49, one study, 63 women) and 600 mg (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.71, one study, 63 women) was more effective than placebo. Ketoprofen 100 mg was also more effective than placebo (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.79, one study, 72 women), but the 50 mg dose showed no significant difference (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.07, one study, 72 women). 3. Combination Analgesics vs. Placebo The pooled analysis showed no significant difference in the need for additional pain relief with combination analgesics compared to placebo (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.40, three trials, 242 women, I² = 69%). Subgroup analysis revealed differences between specific drug combinations. Paracetamol plus codeine reduced the need for additional pain relief (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.82, one trial, 65 women). Paracetamol plus oxycodone and paracetamol plus propoxyphene showed no significant difference compared to placebo (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.28, one trial, 96 women, and RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.11 to 3.69, one trial, 81 women, respectively). Maternal side effects were more common in the combination analgesics group compared to placebo (RR 13.18, 95% CI 2.86 to 60.68, three trials, 252 women). 4. Opioid Analgesics vs. Non-Opioid Analgesics The confidence interval for the effect on additional pain relief between opioid and non-opioid drugs was very wide, indicating uncertainty (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.07 to 3.51, one trial, 121 women). Side effects were more common with opioids compared to non-opioids (RR 2.32, 95% CI 1.15 to 4.69, two trials, 241 women). 5. Opioid Analgesics vs. Combination Analgesics There was no significant difference in the need for additional pain relief between opioid analgesics and combination analgesics (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.07 to 3.51, one study, 121 women). Maternal adverse effects were also similar between the two groups (RR 6.74, 95% CI 0.39 to 116.79). 6. Non-Opioid Analgesics vs. Combination Analgesics Women who received non-opioid analgesics were more likely to require additional pain relief compared to those who received combination analgesics (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.93, one trial, 192 women). Secondary Outcomes No data were available on secondary outcomes such as length of hospital stay, re-hospitalization due to incisional pain, breastfeeding status at discharge, incisional pain at six weeks postpartum, maternal postpartum depression, mother-baby interaction, or cost of treatment. Conclusions The analysis included eight trials with 962 women, but only four trials were of high quality. The small number of studies and participants limits the reliability of the findings. Subgroup analyses were conducted for different drugs and doses, but the data were insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the safest and most effective oral analgesics for post-caesarean pain relief. Further research is needed to address these gaps.
